title: Affidavits when probate is absent for an extra-provincial will
mainQuestion: When an extra-provincial will affecting land has not been granted probate, what affidavits must be registered with the certified copy?
studySummary: When the will referred to in subsection 23(1) has not been granted probate, the certified copy is not registered alone. It must be accompanied by a witness affidavit proving due execution by the testator and an affidavit of the testator's death.

objectives.objective: Recall the affidavits that must accompany the certified copy when probate has not been granted.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must be registered with the certified copy of the will when the will has not been granted probate?
objectives.studyAnswer: An affidavit sworn by one of the witnesses to the will, either within or without the Province, proving due execution by the testator, together with an affidavit of the death of the testator, must be registered with the certified copy.

evidence.evidenceText: 23(2)Where a will referred to in subsection (1) has not been granted probate there shall be registered with the certified copy thereof an affidavit sworn by one of the witnesses to the will, either within or without the Province, proving the due execution thereof by the testator, together with an affidavit of the death of the testator.

title: Registration path for Quebec or South Africa notarial wills
mainQuestion: How may a Quebec or South Africa notarial will be registered, and what supporting affidavits are required?
studySummary: A notarial will under the laws of Quebec or South Africa may be registered in a county registry office as other conveyances are registered. The notarial certified copy must be supported by the officer's affidavit that the will is valid and subsisting where executed, sworn before an authorized person, and it must be accompanied by an affidavit of the testator's death.

objectives.objective: Recall the copy and officer affidavit required for a Quebec or South Africa notarial will.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What copy and officer affidavit are required before a Quebec or South Africa notarial will may be registered?
objectives.studyAnswer: There must be a notarial certified copy with an affidavit of the officer with whom the will is deposited stating that the will is a valid and subsisting will under the laws of the province or country where it was executed, sworn before a person authorized to take proof of instruments out of the Province.

evidence.evidenceText: 23(3)Where a will is a notarial will under the laws of the Province of Quebec or of South Africa, a notarial certified copy thereof with an affidavit of the officer, with whom such will is deposited, that such will is a valid and subsisting will under the laws of the province or country where the same was executed, sworn to before any of the persons authorized to take proof of the execution of instruments out of the Province, may, if it is accompanied by an affidavit of the death of the testator, be registered in the registry office for any county of the Province as other conveyances are registered, and the same when so registered shall have the same effect as if the original will had been registered therein.

objectives.objective: Recall the registration destination, death affidavit condition, and effect of registration.
objectives.guidedQuestion: If the required notarial-will materials are accompanied by an affidavit of death, where may they be registered and with what effect?
objectives.studyAnswer: They may be registered in the registry office for any county of the Province as other conveyances are registered, and when registered they have the same effect as if the original will had been registered there.

evidence.evidenceText: 23(3)Where a will is a notarial will under the laws of the Province of Quebec or of South Africa, a notarial certified copy thereof with an affidavit of the officer, with whom such will is deposited, that such will is a valid and subsisting will under the laws of the province or country where the same was executed, sworn to before any of the persons authorized to take proof of the execution of instruments out of the Province, may, if it is accompanied by an affidavit of the death of the testator, be registered in the registry office for any county of the Province as other conveyances are registered, and the same when so registered shall have the same effect as if the original will had been registered therein.

title: Rent payable by an aquaculture lease holder
mainQuestion: How is the rent payable by an aquaculture lease holder determined?
studySummary: A lease holder must pay rent. The amount is fixed by regulation, whether before or after the lease is granted, and if no applicable regulation exists, the rent is fixed by the Registrar.

objectives.objective: Recall the duty to pay rent and how the amount is fixed.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Who must pay rent for an aquaculture lease, and how is the amount set?
objectives.studyAnswer: The lease holder shall pay rent in an amount fixed by the regulations, whether before or after the grant of the lease; if there is no applicable regulation, the rent is fixed by the Registrar.

title: Special levy amount and member approval
mainQuestion: How is the amount of a special levy determined and approved?
studySummary: The Council determines the amount of the special levy, but that amount must also be approved by voting members present at either the annual general meeting or a special meeting called for that purpose.

objectives.objective: Recall who determines the special levy amount and how member approval is obtained.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Who determines the amount of a special levy, and what member approval is required?
objectives.studyAnswer: The Council determines the amount, and it must be approved at either the annual general meeting or a special meeting called for that purpose by a vote of the voting members present.

title: Instrument receipt, examination, registration, and rejection
mainQuestion: What steps does the registrar follow when an instrument is received, examined, accepted, or rejected for filing or registration?
studySummary: For every instrument received at the land titles office, the registrar records its number, date, and time in the instrument record. The instrument is then examined, an accepted instrument is registered, and the registrar may refuse or reject an instrument for unpaid fees or specified defects such as wrong district, missing approved parcel identifier, retired parcel identifier, improper form, or non-compliance with the Community Planning Act.

objectives.objective: Recall the initial instrument record entry for an instrument received at the land titles office.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the registrar assign and enter when an instrument is received for filing or registration?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar shall assign a registration number, date, and time to every instrument received and enter a record of the instrument, date, time, and number in the instrument record.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(1)The registrar shall assign a registration number, date and time to every instrument received at the land titles office for filing or registration and shall enter a record of the instrument, date, time and number in the instrument record.

objectives.objective: Recall examination, acceptance recording, and registration after acceptance.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What happens after an instrument is recorded as received and then accepted for registration?
objectives.studyAnswer: The instrument is examined and, subject to the rejection power in subsection 18(4), a record of acceptance for filing or registration is entered in the instrument record; when accepted for registration, it shall be registered.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(2)The instrument shall then be examined and, subject to subsection (4), a record of the acceptance of the instrument for filing or registration shall be entered in the instrument record.
18(3)When an instrument is accepted for registration pursuant to subsection (2), it shall be registered.

objectives.objective: Recall the registrar's grounds for refusing, filing, registering, or rejecting an instrument.
objectives.guidedQuestion: On what grounds may the registrar refuse to file or register, and may reject, an instrument?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar may refuse to file or register and may reject an instrument if the appropriate fee has not been paid, or if the instrument does not relate to land in the registrar's district, lacks the approved parcel identifier or is otherwise incomplete, uses a retired parcel identifier or adds a description in addition to the approved parcel identifier, is not in proper form or fit for filing or registration, or does not comply with the Community Planning Act if applicable.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(4)Notwithstanding anything in this or any other enactment, the registrar may refuse to file or register and may reject an instrument where the appropriate fee has not been paid therefor or where the instrument (a) does not relate to land situated in his district; (b) does not describe the land to which it relates by its approved parcel identifier, or is otherwise incomplete; (b.1) describes the land (i) by reference to a parcel identifier that has been marked as retired by the registrar, or (ii) by a description of the land in addition to a reference to its approved parcel identifier; (c) is not in proper form or fit for filing or registration; or (d) does not comply with the Community Planning Act, if applicable.

title: Certificates, Registry Act notice, and parcel identifiers
mainQuestion: What certificate, notice, and parcel identifier steps follow certain title registrations under the Land Titles Act?
studySummary: When the registrar is required to register title, land, ownership, severance, consolidation, or a transfer, the registrar cancels any certificate of registered ownership for that land and issues the required certificate. Certain registrations also require a prescribed Registry Act notice, after which the title is dealt with under this Act, and every registered-title parcel must be identified by its approved parcel identifier in the title register.

objectives.objective: Recall the certificate cancellation and issuance duties tied to specified registrations.
objectives.guidedQuestion: When specified title or land registrations occur, what must the registrar do with certificates of registered ownership?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar shall cancel any certificate of registered ownership for that land and issue a certificate of registered ownership to the owner, surviving owner, personal representative, agent, or trustee, as the case may be; for a subdivision, a certificate is issued for each lot, block, or parcel in the subdivision plan.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(5)Where the registrar is required pursuant to the provisions of this Act to register the title to land or to register land or to register a person as the owner of land or to register an instrument severing or consolidating land or a transfer, the registrar shall (a) cancel the certificate of registered ownership, if any, as to that land; and (b) issue to the owner, surviving owner, personal representative, agent or trustee, as the case may be, a certificate of registered ownership for that land and, in the case of a subdivision, a certificate of registered ownership for each lot, block or parcel in the subdivision plan.

objectives.objective: Recall when a Registry Act notice is issued and the resulting Land Titles Act treatment.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What follows when the registrar registers title under an order under section 12, 13, or 14, or registers title to previously unregistered land under section 23?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar shall issue and record a prescribed-form notice under the Registry Act, and after that the title is dealt with under this Act, which applies to every instrument or document relating to an interest in that land.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(6)Where the registrar registers a title to land pursuant to an order under section 12, 13 or 14 or a title to previously unregistered land pursuant to section 23, the registrar shall issue and record under the Registry Act a notice in prescribed form and thereafter the title to the land shall be dealt with under this Act, and this Act applies to every instrument or document that relates to an interest in that land.

objectives.objective: Recall the approved parcel identifier requirement in the title register.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How must every parcel with title registered under the Act be identified in the title register?
objectives.studyAnswer: Every parcel of land for which title is registered under the Act shall be identified by its approved parcel identifier in the title register.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(7)Every parcel of land in respect of which a title is registered under this Act shall be identified by its approved parcel identifier in the title register.

title: Rejection records, protected instruments, amendments, and Registry Act documents
mainQuestion: What rules govern rejected instruments, protected section 12(10) instruments, amending instruments, and Registry Act documents dealing with land under the Land Titles Act?
studySummary: When an instrument is rejected, the registrar records the rejection and reasons and notifies the presenter. Notwithstanding subsection (4), the registrar must not reject an instrument referred to in subsection 12(10). Filed or registered instruments may be amended by an amending instrument on terms imposed by the registrar, and the Registrar General may order registration under this Act of a Registry Act document sufficient to pass an estate or interest in registered land.

objectives.objective: Recall what the registrar records and whom the registrar notifies after rejecting an instrument.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What must the registrar do upon rejecting an instrument?
objectives.studyAnswer: The registrar shall enter in the instrument record both a record of the rejection and a memorandum of the reasons for it, and shall notify the person who presented the instrument for registration.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(9)Upon the rejection of an instrument, the registrar shall enter in the instrument record a record of the rejection and a memorandum of the reasons for such rejection, and shall notify the person who presented the instrument for registration.

objectives.objective: Recall the instrument that subsection 18(10) protects from rejection.
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which instrument shall the registrar not reject despite the general rejection power?
objectives.studyAnswer: Notwithstanding subsection (4), the registrar shall not reject an instrument referred to in subsection 12(10).

evidence.evidenceText: 18(10)Notwithstanding subsection (4), the registrar shall not reject an instrument referred to in subsection 12(10).

objectives.objective: Recall how a filed or registered instrument may be amended.
objectives.guidedQuestion: How may an instrument filed or registered under the Act be amended?
objectives.studyAnswer: It may, subject to terms and conditions imposed by the registrar, be amended by filing or registering an amending instrument in prescribed form.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(11)Any instrument that is filed or registered under this Act may, subject to such terms and conditions as the registrar may impose, be amended by the filing or registration of an amending instrument in prescribed form.

objectives.objective: Recall the Registrar General's discretionary authority for Registry Act documents dealing with land registered under the Act.
objectives.guidedQuestion: What may the Registrar General order when a Registry Act document sufficient to pass an estate or interest deals with land registered under the Land Titles Act?
objectives.studyAnswer: The Registrar General may, in absolute discretion, order the proper registrar to register the document under the Land Titles Act; when so registered, it has the same effect as if registered as an instrument.

evidence.evidenceText: 18(12)Notwithstanding anything in this Act, where a document sufficient to pass an estate or interest in land under the Registry Act deals with land registered under this Act, the Registrar General may, in his absolute discretion, order the proper registrar to register it under this Act, and when so registered it shall have the same effect as if registered as an instrument.

title: Planning and development regulation subjects
mainQuestion: What subjects may planning and development regulations address under subsection 125(1)?
studySummary: Subsection 125(1) authorizes regulations across many planning and development subjects, including setbacks, mobile home parks, automotive facilities, advertising signs, excavation, subdivision, lot standards, wastewater, pool fences, building and structure work, development approvals, wiring permit restrictions linked to approvals, land use and development policies, designated-area matters that councils may address by by-law except development schemes, and anything else otherwise authorized by the Act. Because the approved focus spans the full catalogue, it should be split before approval as a durable study unit.

objectives.objective: Recall the physical siting and facility-specific subjects listed in subsection 125(1).
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which physical siting and facility-specific subjects may regulations address under subsection 125(1)?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may govern setbacks of buildings and structures from street boundaries, prescribe mobile home park location, layout, equipment, standards, licensing, site standards and operator fees, prescribe location and dimensions of service stations, gas bars, car washes and automotive repair garages and approve construction standards, regulate public advertising signs and billboards, and govern commercial excavation of listed deposits.

objectives.objective: Recall the land division, lot, wastewater, and pool fence subjects listed in subsection 125(1).
objectives.guidedQuestion: Which subdivision, lot, wastewater, and pool fence subjects may regulations address?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may respect subdividing land, govern the location and dimensions of and residential density for lots, govern wastewater disposal, and govern the location and construction of pool fences.

objectives.objective: Recall the building work, development approval, and wiring permit subjects listed in subsection 125(1).
objectives.guidedQuestion: What building work, development approval, and wiring permit matters may regulations address?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may address building, dimensions, locating or relocating, demolishing, altering, structurally altering, repairing or replacing buildings and structures, including standards and prohibitions on violating them. They may also address development approvals, including applications, granting, suspending, reinstating and revoking approvals, forms, terms and conditions, fees, building inspection service fees, information to the Executive Director of Assessment and use of that information. In an area where paragraph (g) or (h) regulations are in effect, they may prohibit issuing an electrical wiring permit for a development unless the applicant delivers a copy of the development approval.

objectives.objective: Recall the policy, designated-area, and residual regulation subjects listed in subsection 125(1).
objectives.guidedQuestion: What policy, designated-area, and residual subjects may regulations address?
objectives.studyAnswer: Regulations may respect land use and development policies, including policies on settlement patterns, commercial and industrial siting, parking, loading zones, flood plains, and coastal-zone planning. In an area designated under subsection (3), they may govern anything, except a development scheme, or a combination of things that a council is empowered to do by by-law under the Act. They may also respect anything otherwise authorized by the Act.
